newsitem.title: UK: N.Europe beet crop seen down after adverse weather.
newsitem.headline: N.Europe beet crop seen down after adverse weather.

text.p: Production prospects for northern European beet growers, the mainstay of the European Union's (EU) 1996/97 sugar crop, are still mixed as recent rainfall balanced the effects of an earlier drought and adverse spring weather.
Analysts say cold dry conditions after drilling, followed by dry weather in July and August, have hampered beet development although many areas have since received much-needed moisture.
Estimates for this year's crop show a marginal decline over 1995/96 with trade house Czarnikow tentatively pegging output at 16.8 million tonnes raw value after a previous 17.02 million.
European Commission officials said as the harvest is still in progress, production estimates were still provisional and likely to be revised.
"French figures, based on their beet test, may fall by some 150,000 tonnes and an expected increase in the German crop is unlikely to be as great," an EU official said.
Another official said the 1996/97 estimates were especially chaotic due to weather conditions during the growing season.
France, the EU's largest beet grower, should produce less sugar this year than in 1995 as results of the fourth beet field test show that the crop has made only a partial recovery.
The French sugar intervention board FIRS said on Monday it was maintaining its estimate of 3.9 million tonnes for the 1996/97 crop after the fourth and last test on September 13.
France produced 4.2 million tonnes of sugar in 1995/96.
"We are holding our forecast of a sugar yield of 9.4 tonnes per hectare and of a sugar crop of below four million tonnes, assuming an area of 422,000 hectares," a FIRS official said.
Analysts said insufficient moisture between the third and fourth tests had limited the crop's progress.
In Germany, the fourth test result published on Monday showed implied sugar yields had progressed over the last two weeks and should support a better final crop figure.
A sugar yield of 9.71 tonnes per hectare compared with 8.78 tonnes in the fourth test last year.
"It doesn't look unfavourable any more, sugar production could now exceed earlier forecasts if we get the right mixture of rainfall and sunshine during the beet campaign," said one.

"Beet leaves are healthy and leaf weight is high, which points to reasonable sugar contents, although it is uncertain at what stage they will be reached given the rain pattern," a spokesman for the WVZ sugar association said last week.
WVZ, which collects the national data, is maintaining its output forecast at 3.87 million tonnes, up 1.9 percent.
Sugar yields in the first two tests this year were down, reflecting drought in the spring, but the third test was more promising after rainy weather in August aided crop development.
In the latest test, sugar contents and beet weights were both higher than last year, with good plant densities also pointing to higher sugar yields.
In Britain, the recent rains over beet growing areas have helped reverse the effects of the earlier dry weather and the initial gloomy prognosis for this year's crop.
Amounts of sugar per root and root weights are now above 1995 levels, although sugar contents are still lagging behind.
"It (the crop) is making nice progress...it's promising. The rains in the recent weeks...have been just what the crop needs," said an official at the National Farmers Union (NFU).
British Sugar has said the crop has made good progress and is on course for an average result but has declined to give any output estimate or the number of beets sown per hectare.
Sugar output in another of the region's leading growers, the Netherlands, is also expected to be slightly lower this year due to the dry weather, although the rains have also helped.
According to leading producer Suiker Unie, which produces around 65 percent of Dutch beet, the rains in late August compensated for a dry summer and improved crop potential.

"We were very happy that the rain came, the leaf on the crop looks very healthy," said Alfons Calon, the company's agricultural affairs director. He estimated output at or just above one million tonnes, after 1.074 million tonnes in 1995/96.
Belgium and other Benelux countries are only about one per cent down on last year according to their beet test results despite early drought and late rain.
